source.title: Performance Law of Large Language Models

record.file_problem: Text is substantially complete. Some figure labels are garbled, but the relevant figure metrics and descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream-score predictability using MMLU predictions from an empirical performance equation, rather than held-out cross-entropy loss or the original scaling-law measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper predicts MMLU scores for named models and compares them with reported scores; those comparisons are recorded below. Its 7B and 141B examples and other application examples are formula outputs, not observed model outcomes. Scaling-law results cited from other work are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study fits a log-linear equation in depth, width, FFN size and effective training tokens on 10 models from 2024. It compares predicted with reported MMLU for 55 models (Table 1) plus 2 later models (Appendix A). That bears on whether downstream performance is predictable from scale (V6). It does not measure pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim a simple MMLU 'performance law' fitted on 10 models from 2024 predicts MMLU accurately across sizes, years and organisations, especially for English models. They attribute Llama1's overprediction and Chinese-enhanced models' underprediction to differences in exam-like data. They question how much progress has been made beyond accumulating more data. The paper is labelled as the authors' personal opinions.
record.recipe_differences: Predicts MMLU using a log-linear equation of architecture variables and effective training tokens, fitted on 10 open-source 2024 models; it does not fit held-out cross-entropy scaling laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The equation explicitly includes layer count, hidden size, FFN size, effective training tokens, and a precision/instability coefficient γ. The authors discuss data quality, model shape, precision, and training strategy as sources of prediction differences.
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper does not state a held-out evaluation split for the 55-model comparison; it fits parameters on 10 2024 models and compares predictions with reported benchmark results. Some architecture values in Table 1 are marked as guesses, and the authors note that some are probably inaccurate. MMLU prediction does not directly test held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: None. The formula-only examples in sections 2.2 and 3 are not observed model outcomes and were excluded.

untested.parts: All: no held-out pretraining loss is measured.
All: no loss laws fitted on small runs are extrapolated. The MMLU fit uses 7B–405B models, not small runs.
All: no compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is derived. The T'=min(T,S) saturation clip is assumed, not tested.
No controlled shape comparison. The authors only assert, from practice and regression coefficients, that same-size models differ by shape. Figure 2 is formula output.
All: text LLMs only. The model-expansion example (3.4) is formula output.

Prediction from pretraining loss. Controlled scale sweeps within one training recipe. Held-out evaluation for 2024 models: the 10 fitting models are among the Table 1 rows and are not identified. Benchmarks other than MMLU: the MMLU-Pro mapping and BIG-Bench correlation are given without accuracy numbers.
All: no comparison of exponents or allocations across fitting choices.

missing.what: Real vs predicted metric over training tokens for two of the authors' own models. One tracks the prediction; one deviates, with inferred γ≈3.7 traced to implementation bugs. No numbers are given.
Linear mapping from MMLU to MMLU-Pro (y=2.33x−133) for MMLU>70, and a claimed 'very high correlation' with BIG-Bench. No fit statistics are reported.
Which 10 models were used for fitting, and that contamination-checked models were up-sampled. Needed to separate in-sample from out-of-sample rows.

record.verdict_notes: Preprint without uncertainty estimates. Table 1 rows mix in-sample fitting points (unidentified) with held-out predictions; only r56 and r57 are clearly out-of-sample. The paper's statements on depth, hidden size versus FFN size, and MoE come from regression coefficients and formula outputs (Figures 2–3), not controlled experiments, so they are not counted as a test of V4. The reader's state threshold is slightly inconsistent: a −4.49 gap is observed (r40) while +5.06 is partial (r45). This was left as is.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether loss laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count and loss.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
The paper predicts MMLU from architecture and training-data inputs, not performance from pretraining loss; it does not establish a downstream-task improvement curve across controlled scale changes.
No comparison of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations under alternative counting, schedules, data, or fitting methods.

relationships.condition: Most models across families and years, including the 2 models released after the paper
relationships.reason: Predicted MMLU is within about ±3–4.5 points of reported scores for most models (r7–r11, r13–r34, r36, r37, r39–r44, r46–r48). It is within ~2 points for the out-of-sample OLMoE and MiniCPM3 (r56, r57). Some of these rows use guessed inputs, and some 2024 models may be in the fitting set.
relationships.display_finding: Predictions were within about 3–4.5 points for most models and about 2 points for held-out OLMoE and MiniCPM3, although some inputs were guessed and fitting-set membership was uncertain.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Most models across families and years, including the 2 models released after the paper
source_check.reason: Table 1 shows close agreement for the cited condition group. Appendix A reports OLMoE at 54.1 versus 56.21 predicted and MiniCPM3 at 67.2 versus 65.36 predicted. Guessed inputs and fitting-set overlap weaken the validation.

relationships.condition: First-generation Llama, early small models (Llama2 7B/13B, Gemma 2B, Qwen 1.8B): overpredicted
relationships.reason: Reported MMLU falls 6–19 points below prediction (r1–r3, r5, r6, r12, r35), with a 4.9-point gap at Llama 65B (r4). The authors attribute this to less exam-like training data, so scale variables alone miss data-mix effects.
relationships.display_finding: MMLU scores fell 6–19 points below predictions, with a 4.9-point gap for Llama 65B, which the authors attributed to less exam-like training data.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: First-generation Llama, early small models (Llama2 7B/13B, Gemma 2B, Qwen 1.8B): overpredicted
source_check.reason: Table 1 shows systematic overprediction, including r1's 19.19-point gap and a 4.94-point gap for Llama 65B. These exceptions qualify cross-model prediction; they do not establish absent scaling.

relationships.condition: Chinese-enhanced models (Qwen 72B, Qwen1.5 72B, Qwen2, Yi, GLM-4): underpredicted
relationships.reason: Reported MMLU exceeds prediction by 5–8 points (r38, r45, r49–r55). The authors attribute this to a higher share of exam data, so the prediction depends on the data mix.
relationships.display_finding: MMLU scores exceeded predictions by 5–8 points, which the authors attributed to a higher proportion of exam data.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Chinese-enhanced models (Qwen 72B, Qwen1.5 72B, Qwen2, Yi, GLM-4): underpredicted
source_check.reason: The cited Table 1 rows exceed predictions by 5.06–8.26 points, including r49's 7.57-point gap. Section 2.3 proposes a greater share of exam-like data as an explanation.

relation.reason: Its predicted-versus-reported MMLU comparisons directly bear on V6.

tranche.reason: The study tests downstream predictability using a cross-model MMLU regression rather than the original pretraining-loss scaling method.

source_check.notes: The ten fitting models are not individually identified, so Table 1 is not an entirely identifiable held-out evaluation. Starred architecture or token inputs are author guesses; data-mixture explanations are observational hypotheses.

statements.correction: Table 1: Llama 7B predicted 54.29, reported 35.1; Qwen 2 7B predicted 62.73, reported 70.3. Predictor: architecture variables and effective training tokens, with MoE adjustments. V6 verdict for these conditions: limits_scope. Sections 2.3 and 4.1: proposed training-data explanations.
statements.problem: The cited numbers are correct, but these residuals qualify the fitted equation's portability rather than establish absent or reversed downstream predictability. Data-mixture explanations are proposed, not causally demonstrated.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Overall reported-model comparison and English models excluding Llama1
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports strong aggregate agreement between predicted and reported MMLU scores (r = 0.925, MAE = 3.780 overall; r = 0.963, MAE = 2.486 for the stated English subset), with the model comparisons in r1–r59.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: First-generation Llama models and models with larger individual table discrepancies
reader_labels.reason: The authors say first-generation Llama scores are well below prediction; several table comparisons also show appreciable differences, including Qwen 2 7B, Qwen 2 72B, Qwen 2 57B-A14B, Yi 34B, and Yi-1.5 34B (r1–r4, r49–r55).
